evaluation.positioning_hook: A grieving Catholic father hunts the family that destroyed his home, while his cop sister races to stop him before vengeance, faith, and bloodline collide in one final reckoning.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The revenge-crime engine is easy to grasp and the emotional stakes are immediate, but the script’s heavy Catholic theology, family tragedy, and brutal violence narrow the audience. The hook is commercial enough for adult thriller buyers, not broad four-quadrant play.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands fast: a devastated brother/father becomes an avenger, while his police-officer sister sits on the other side of the law. The Risaldi family, the church/confession framework, and the countdown to the mansion showdown give the story a clean, readable engine.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Jacob and Jodie are both built around pain, duty, and contradiction, and Ethan adds a morally unstable counterweight that keeps scenes alive. Victor is a strong villain engine, though the supporting family members are more functional than fully dimensional.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s Catholic ritual structure, confession framing, and repeated use of hymns and sacred spaces give the material a distinct identity. It’s still operating inside a familiar revenge-crime lane, but the spiritual register makes the execution feel authored.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The opening massacre, the alley confrontation, and the club finale all create strong forward motion, and the story keeps tightening around the Risaldi family. Some midsection scenes lean on dialogue-heavy moral debate, but the escalation stays clear and the endgame is well signposted.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea is familiar in shape but fresh in texture: a Catholic grief story that turns into a family-vs-family crime purge. The confession booth, adoration chapel, and hymn motifs make the revenge arc feel spiritually specific rather than generic.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The script builds a specific social world around church life, police bureaucracy, criminal hierarchy, and family ritual. The Risaldi mansion, the club, the docks, and the church all feel like parts of one ecosystem rather than isolated set pieces.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unusually committed: mournful, devotional, and violent, with sacred imagery constantly colliding with brutality. That blend is consistent from the opening song sequence through the confession scenes and the final blood-soaked ballroom.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There’s real thematic depth in the script’s obsession with guilt, absolution, inherited violence, and what justice means when the law fails. The Victor/Ethan/Jacob triangle suggests more psychological material than the plot alone needs.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The script gets a lot of mileage out of sibling, parent-child, and surrogate-father relationships, and multiple pairings generate distinct energy. Jacob/Jodie, Ethan/Victor, Ethan/Frankie, and Jacob/Father Michael all feel like playable recurring dynamics.

lead_characters.name: Jacob Smith
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 30s to early 40s, Catholic, working-class father and older brother.
lead_characters.hook: A devout, emotionally shattered family man who starts as a grieving survivor and becomes a vengeance engine. He’s gentle in the home, feral in the street, and the script keeps testing whether his faith is a restraint, a refuge, or a justification.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Casey Affleck in Manchester by the Sea or Joel Edgerton in The Gift — a role built on contained grief, moral collapse, and the slow turn from restraint to violence. It gives an actor a full-spectrum emotional arc, from devotional tenderness to blood-soaked fury.

lead_characters.name: Jodie Smith
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late 30s, police officer, Catholic, Jacob’s sister.
lead_characters.hook: A work-driven cop who is trying to keep her brother alive while carrying her own grief and professional guilt. She’s the script’s pressure valve and moral counterweight, but she’s also personally implicated, which makes every scene with Jacob feel loaded.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Amy Ryan in Gone Baby Gone or Regina King in If Beale Street Could Talk real heat — a woman balancing authority, heartbreak, and family loyalty. It offers a strong emotional close-up and a grounded procedural presence.

lead_characters.name: Ethan Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 20s, Catholic, morally conflicted member of the Risaldi family.
lead_characters.hook: The family’s conscience, or at least the closest thing to one, Ethan is torn between loyalty, revulsion, and a desperate need to believe he can still choose differently. He’s the most volatile supporting role in the script because he can pivot from informant to accomplice to spiritual witness in a single scene.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Michael Shannon in Take Shelter or Jesse Plemons in Breaking Bad — a role where internal fracture is the performance. It gives an actor the chance to play fear, shame, intelligence, and moral awakening without ever becoming passive.

lead_characters.name: Victor Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 60s, patriarch, organized-crime boss, physically composed and intimidating.
lead_characters.hook: A cold patriarch who treats his sons like disposable assets and uses shame as a weapon. He is less a gangster than an ideology of domination, and the script gives him the kind of authority that can freeze a room before he even raises his voice.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Bryan Cranston in Breaking Bad or Michael Keaton in The Founder a chance to weaponize charisma and menace at once. It’s a prestige-villain part with real scene-commanding power.

lead_characters.name: Father Michael
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 50s, Catholic priest, compassionate and wise.
lead_characters.hook: A priest who functions as spiritual guide, confidant, and thematic chorus. He’s not just there to counsel; he gives the movie its moral vocabulary and helps translate the violence into a faith-based framework.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Mark Rylance in Bridge of Spies or Brendan Gleeson in Calvary its quiet authority — a man whose stillness carries the weight of the film. It offers a rich, text-driven performance with warmth and gravitas.

lead_characters.name: Frankie Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 20s to early 30s, criminal family member, physically capable, emotionally suppressed.
lead_characters.hook: A soldier in the family machine who still has enough conscience left to crack under pressure. He’s one of the script’s most tragic secondary figures because he seems closest to escape and still can’t get out alive.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Ben Foster in Hell or High Water or Paul Dano in Prisoners a chance to play panic under discipline. It’s a tense, emotionally volatile part with a real breakdown payoff.

lead_characters.name: Martin Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 30s, violent criminal enforcer, physically imposing.
lead_characters.hook: The family’s most overtly sadistic son, Martin is the face of brutality before the script reveals the deeper rot underneath him. He’s a terrifying antagonist because he’s not just cruel — he’s desperate to be seen as what his father made him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Jack O’Connell in Starred Up or Walton Goggins in Justified a chance to be dangerous, wounded, and magnetic. It’s a high-intensity villain part with strong scene-stealing potential.

lead_characters.name: Alicia
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid 50s, Victor’s wife, former stripper, mother of the Risaldi sons.
lead_characters.hook: A woman trapped inside the family’s hierarchy, trying to survive a marriage built on humiliation and control. She’s one of the script’s clearest victims of Victor’s worldview, and her presence gives the family structure a tragic domestic dimension.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Patricia Clarkson in Sharp Objects or Laura Linney in Ozark a chance to play quiet damage under pressure. It offers a painful, contained performance with real emotional residue.

lead_characters.name: Marcus Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: The “pure” child the family mythologizes, Marcus is the one innocent body the script keeps protecting until the end. He’s less a character with dialogue than a moral object the story keeps circling, which makes his presence feel loaded every time he appears.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: For a child actor, this is the kind of role that gives a film its emotional center without requiring a lot of dialogue. It’s a memorable, symbolic part that can leave a strong impression with very little screen time.

casting_characteristics: one child role with sustained emotional significance
multiple male roles in late 20s to late 60s
physically imposing criminal roles for the Risaldi brothers

notable_requirements: large mansion ballroom and private rooms

technical.vfx_details: Mostly practical production with limited cleanup, smoke/fire enhancement, and a few stylized transition moments.
technical.sfx_needs: Gunshots, blood effects, a child death sequence, fire/burning evidence, and practical violence in confined spaces.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: premium streaming or theatrical specialty crime drama
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: adult prestige crime thriller with awards-adjacent dramatic positioning and a strong streaming afterlife.

budget.note: Contemporary and mostly practical, but the script needs multiple night exteriors, a large mansion set, a club sequence, docks/warehouse destruction, smoke/fire work, and a sizable child-protection-heavy finale.

casting.note: Jacob, Jodie, Victor, Ethan, and Martin all need sharply differentiated emotional registers, and the child role of Marcus has to land as more than symbolic weight. The Risaldi brothers also need a family resemblance and a credible criminal hierarchy.

development.note: The script’s faith-and-vengeance framework is distinctive, but the dense family mythology, repeated moral speeches, and multiple reversals around who knows what will need careful clarity in packaging conversations.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who respond to prestige crime dramas with moral weight, Catholic imagery, and emotionally punishing family stakes.
audience_target.demographics: 25-54, slightly male-skewing but viable with women 35+; higher tolerance for bleak material, faith themes, and violent crime drama.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary locations, limited VFX, and a contained cast keep it in indie feature territory, though the club, docks, and mansion sequences add scope.

lane_fit.lane: prestige crime thriller with spiritual overtones
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of adult crime stories that use family trauma and moral philosophy as the engine. The Catholic iconography and grief-forward lead role make it especially attractive to buyers looking for elevated genre with a serious performance centerpiece.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with a closed revenge arc and no clear spinoff vector beyond the central family story.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Catholic ritual gives the movie a signature spine.
strengths.what_it_means: That spiritual framework makes the script easier to position than a generic revenge thriller because it has a recognizable thematic identity and a built-in emotional vocabulary. Buyers chasing elevated genre, faith-adjacent drama, and awards-friendly crime material will immediately understand the lane.
strengths.evidence: Confession booth scenes, adoration chapel scenes, Father Michael’s sermons, and repeated use of hymns and prayer language.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Jacob is a serious actor role.
strengths.what_it_means: The lead is built for a performer who can carry grief, rage, restraint, and spiritual collapse in one package, which is exactly what gets packages moving. This is the kind of part that attracts prestige character actors and can anchor the entire buy.
strengths.evidence: Jacob’s therapy breakdown, the alley fight, the confession scene, and the final confrontation with Victor.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The family-vs-family engine is clean and playable.
strengths.what_it_means: The script gives producers a simple commercial engine: one devastated family versus the criminal family that destroyed them. That clarity helps marketing, casting, and trailer construction because the conflict is legible without explanation.
strengths.evidence: The Risaldi home invasion, the alley confrontation, the mansion showdown, and the repeated police briefings.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ensemble has real relationship heat.
strengths.what_it_means: Multiple pairings generate distinct scenes, which gives the project more than one casting lane and more than one emotional entry point. That makes it easier to sell as actor-driven prestige material rather than a one-note revenge piece.
strengths.evidence: Jacob/Jodie, Ethan/Victor, Ethan/Frankie, Jacob/Father Michael, and Victor/Alicia all carry different dramatic textures.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ending is built for catharsis and debate.
strengths.what_it_means: The final ballroom sequence resolves the plot while leaving the audience with a moral question, which is valuable for word of mouth and post-screening conversation. Buyers like endings that feel decisive but not simplistic, especially in prestige crime.
strengths.evidence: Victor’s confession of control, Jacob’s near-execution, Jodie’s intervention, and the final movement toward confession and peace.

whats_special.headline: This is a prestige crime feature with a real identity: Catholic ritual, family trauma, and revenge all locked into one clean engine. It has the kind of lead role, tonal specificity, and contained production footprint that can attract an actor-driven package and a buyer looking for elevated adult genre.

items.area: The script leans hard on speeches.
items.detail: Several key scenes turn into extended moral argument — especially Jacob/Jodie in the apartment, Ethan/Victor in the mansion, and Father Michael’s sermon passages. That gives the film thematic weight, but it also creates a buyer concern that the momentum depends on dialogue intensity more than scene-to-scene escalation.

items.area: The opening massacre is extremely punishing.
items.detail: The child death, family execution, and graphic home-invasion sequence establish the stakes fast, but they also set a very hard content ceiling for audience reach and buyer comfort. This is the kind of opening that immediately narrows the lane to mature premium buyers.

items.area: Victor’s family tree is dense on first pass.
items.detail: Martin, Tyler, Frankie, Edward, Ethan, Marcus, Alicia, and Victor all enter with overlapping roles and similar criminal context, which can make the family hierarchy harder to track in a cold read. The script ultimately clarifies the structure, but the early pages ask the audience to do a lot of sorting.

items.area: The music clearance stack is real.
items.detail: The script names multiple songs — including Come Back, O Holy Night, Let All Mortal Flesh Keep Silent, Clair de Lune, 500 Miles, Good Looking, and L’amour Toujours — and several are woven into key emotional beats. That creates a meaningful sync-clearance and budget conversation before greenlight.

issues.headline: The main friction is not the premise — it’s the density of the writing style and the amount of dialogue-driven moral framing the script asks the audience to absorb. Add the severe opening violence and the named-music clearance stack, and this becomes a very specific buyer conversation rather than a broad one.
